forecast_reasoning: Strong spine (fair rules, unfair outcome, why, objections, one fix), a visible proof from second one and a real fight topic; held under 85 because 'every time' and 'most honest picture' overclaim what the toy model shows, the toy-versus-real gap (ninety percent versus thirty-two percent) is never admitted, c07 is a citation dump, and the Skeptic has no payoff.

gap_to_gate.problem: Overclaim. Claim data: across 300 worlds the leader's share at 6,000 flips each ranged 33.5 to 99 percent, median 85. 'Every single time' and 'every world ends the same way. One stack eats the board' are false for the low end. Title 'One Winner. Every Time.' has the same problem. A hostile commenter finds this in one sentence and the whole video is discredited.
gap_to_gate.fix: l04: 'Not sometimes. We played it three hundred times, and in every single one, one stack ended far ahead of the rest.' | l24 (last three sentences): 'Every one of the sixty-four squares won at least once. In every world, the top stack held a third of the board or more. In half of them, more than eighty-five percent.' | Title: 'A Fair Coin Game Ends With One Rich Player. 300 Out Of 300.'

gap_to_gate.problem: Biggest missing step. The toy board ends at ninety percent for one stack; real United States data in l44 says thirty-two percent for the top one percent. Any smart commenter says the model is wrong or exaggerated, and the script never says so. Without this the video looks like it hides the gap.
gap_to_gate.fix: Insert after l45: 'Our toy board ends far worse than the real one. Real countries have taxes, inheritance rules, death and second chances. The toy board has none of that. It shows a direction, not a size.'

gap_to_gate.problem: 'The most honest picture we have of how people get rich' is an unprovable superlative and invites 'it is a toy' as the first comment; 'hate it' is mild bait. It also gives no reason to stay past minute one.
gap_to_gate.fix: 'I will show you every flip that matters. Then I will show you what this toy board can say about how people get rich, and where it cannot. Some of you are going to hate it.'

gap_to_gate.problem: Weakest sixty seconds of the video (l41 to l45, about one hundred and thirty words of citation and percentages, abstract picture of pawns changing size). c06 ends on a high (l40) and c07 opens with a statement, not a question. Viewer leaves at l41 ('three Italian physicists... forty years') or at l44's two percentages. Also 'almost never the most talented' is stronger than the paper.
gap_to_gate.fix: l41: 'Is this only a toy? Three Italian physicists built a bigger one in twenty eighteen. A thousand people. Forty years. Talent spread like real life: most in the middle, a few brilliant.' | l43: 'After forty years, the richest person in the model was rarely the most talented one. It was somebody close to average, who kept getting lucky.' | l44: cut 'The bottom half hold about two and a half percent' from the spoken line and let the tag carry it, or keep and add 1.5 s silence.

gap_to_gate.problem: The whole result rests on the stake rule (one fifth of the poorer stack), which the script chose. l08 sells it as 'as fair as a bet gets'. A commenter says the rule is rigged. The script needs to own the choice here, once, before c06.
gap_to_gate.fix: Append after l30: 'I chose this stake rule. Change the rule and the size of the effect changes. Keep that in mind, because the real world is not this board.'

gap_to_gate.problem: The comparison is stacked: the Heir gets ten times the coins, the Scholar a 55 to 45 edge, and the listener has no baseline. Six in a hundred sounds tiny but a plain player's chance is one in sixty-four (about one and a half). A smart reader says 'you chose the numbers'. l40's 'nobody gets ten lifetimes' is a dodge without the admission.
gap_to_gate.fix: l37: 'The Scholar, with a real edge on every single flip? Six. A plain player gets one and a half.' | l40: 'Talent is not useless. Let the game run ten times longer and the Scholar becomes the most likely winner. But nobody gets ten lifetimes. And yes, I chose these numbers. Change them, and the order changes.'

gap_to_gate.problem: Leap from the toy to politics. The fix rule takes one percent every round forever, which is no real tax; a fitted model matching data is not proof of cause; 'matched within a fraction of a percent' is fact-check pending; 'two weeks ago' dates the video and breaks the moment it is a month old. This is the exact weak spot a hostile commenter attacks.
gap_to_gate.fix: l58: 'Still winners. Still losers. Still unequal. But the game never ends. This rule is not a real tax. It takes one percent every round, forever. It only shows that a steady flow back stops the king.' | l59: 'A mathematician named Bruce Boghosian added a rule like this to the model and fitted it to real wealth data from the United States. The fit was close. A close fit does not prove the cause. It does mean the toy is not nonsense.' | l60: 'That is the argument underneath every fight about taxing the very rich. In November twenty twenty-six, California voted on a one-time five percent tax on billionaires. It lost, fifty-three to forty-seven.' (drop l60 if the vote result is not confirmed on a primary page)

gap_to_gate.problem: 'Scholars exist' equates self-made billionaires with skill alone. That hands the 'merit wins' side an easy win and goes soft against the video's own claim. It also adds no new point after l46.
gap_to_gate.fix: 'And to be fair, in the same year a hundred and ninety-six people got there by building something, and together they made more than the heirs did. Skill is real. But nobody counts the equally good builders who never got lucky.'

gap_to_gate.problem: 'The coin picks the winner' contradicts l40 (given ten times longer, the Scholar wins). l53 also sounds like an ending, so c09 starts with no open question and a viewer who feels finished leaves at the l54 reset.
gap_to_gate.fix: l53 (last two sentences): 'But among the people at the table, luck decides far more than anyone likes. And the coin does not check who deserved it. So can anything stop the king?' | l54 stays unchanged.

notes.comment_fights: Sentences people will argue with: l62 ('Being rich does not prove you were better'), l63 ('being broke does not prove you played badly'), l53 ('the coin does not check who deserved it'), l38 ('Working harder at a coin flip is just more coin flips'), l60 (billionaire tax). All stated hard enough, and l62 to l64 are the right spine. They are true only as a statement about the toy model; the honest-limits part (l40, l47, c08) is currently not enough, because the model-versus-reality size gap (ninety versus thirty-two percent), the chosen stake rule, the chosen Heir/Scholar numbers and the one-percent-forever fix rule are never admitted. The fixes above add those four admissions in one sentence each, so the video stays hard and gets harder to dismiss without going soft. l62 also reads a touch too universal: 'it proves you were at the table, good enough to play, and the coin liked you early' is fine in the toy but a hostile reader will say 'rich people also work'; l47 and l53 now carry that.
